D1_static_migration_guard.exemption_escape_hatch: DELIBERATELY ABSENT. check_migration_accretion honours '-- MIGRATION-ACCRETION-EXEMPTION: ' because accretion is a BUDGET an author may knowingly spend. The TC-11 pin is TERMINAL-FOREVER, not a budget; a hatch would defeat it. Test `pin_has_no_exemption_escape_hatch` asserts a MARKED offender is rejected identically to an unmarked one. Changing the pin is an HITL decision, not a comment.
D1_static_migration_guard.conservatism_recorded: The guard refuses ANY write into logical_id on a canonical table, including a copy that would merely PRESERVE the value through a table-recreate. Distinguishing 'preserving copy' from 'minting copy' requires positional matching of an INSERT column list against a SELECT expression list — fragile, and trivially gamed by exactly the change class the pin exists to stop. A future canonical-table recreate follows step 23's SHIPPED precedent (declare the column; do not copy rows through it) or returns to the HITL. Documented in the fn doc comment under '# Deliberately conservative'.
D1_static_migration_guard.known_limits_recorded: Lexical guard, not a SQL parser. Normalises comments away, elides string literals, unwraps quoted identifiers, splits on ';'. A CREATE TRIGGER body therefore splits into fragments — harmless, because both the CREATE TRIGGER head and any UPDATE ... SET logical_id fragment inside it are independently rejected. Cannot see through dynamically-built SQL, which migrations never use (MIGRATIONS holds &'static str literals).

finding.title: Handle schema-qualified canonical table names
finding.statement: When a migration schema-qualifies the table (e.g. `UPDATE main.canonical_nodes SET logical_id = ...` or `INSERT INTO main.canonical_nodes(logical_id) ...`), SQLite targets the same pinned table, but the guard compared the extracted token LITERALLY against CANONICAL_NODES / CANONICAL_EDGES. The token became MAIN.CANONICAL_NODES, so the pin SILENTLY ACCEPTED the exact backfill shape it is meant to reject.
finding.assessment: Genuine evasion hole in a TERMINAL-FOREVER pin. Reproduced at RED before fixing. A SECOND, related hole was found while writing the tests and closed in the same fix: SQLite's tokenizer also accepts whitespace around the qualifier dot (`UPDATE main . canonical_nodes SET ...`), and the guard's token extractors cut at whitespace, so that spelling extracted the bare token MAIN and slipped the pin too.

sqlite_behaviour_verified_before_asserti.why: The prompt required verifying the whitespace-around-the-dot spelling against real SQLite before asserting on it.
sqlite_behaviour_verified_before_asserti.engine: SQLite 3.45.1 (python3 sqlite3 module, live statements against a real in-memory DB)
results: `INSERT INTO main . t(a) VALUES(1)` — ACCEPTED, targets main.t
`UPDATE main . t SET a=2` — ACCEPTED
`UPDATE temp . t SET a=7` — ACCEPTED
`INSERT INTO "main".t(a) VALUES(4)` / `INSERT INTO [main].[t](a) VALUES(5)` / ``INSERT INTO `temp`.t(a) VALUES(8)`` — ACCEPTED
`UPDATE main.temp.t SET a=1` — SYNTAX ERROR ('near "."'). SQLite permits AT MOST ONE qualifier, which is why `bare_table_name` takes the part after the (single) dot.
sqlite_behaviour_verified_before_asserti.consequence: The whitespace spelling IS asserted on (it parses). No spelling SQLite rejects is asserted on.

findings.title: Handle SQLite UPDATE conflict clauses
findings.statement: For `UPDATE OR <conflict-action> canonical_nodes SET logical_id = ...`, the guard extracted `OR` as the table name and returned false, so a forbidden logical_id backfill bypassed the TERMINAL-FOREVER TC-11 pin.
findings.assessment: GENUINE BYPASS. Reproduced at RED before fixing.
findings.fix: New private fn `update_target_table(statement)` replaces `token_after(statement, "UPDATE ")`. It strips the `UPDATE ` prefix, then skips an optional `OR <action> ` where <action> is one of the five SQLite conflict actions, matched TOKEN-EXACTLY (whole token followed by a single space), then takes the first identifier token. `token_after` and the new `update_target_table` share the extracted helper `first_token`.
findings.insert_arm_checked: The analogous `INSERT OR <action> INTO ...` shape was checked and does NOT have the hole: the INSERT/REPLACE arm anchors on ` INTO `, which the conflict clause precedes, so `table_after_into` already read the real table. Confirmed at RED — pin_rejects_insert_with_an_or_conflict_clause PASSED before the GREEN change — and pinned as a regression test anyway (15 offender shapes: 5 actions x {column list, qualified, no column list}).

findings.title: Avoid substring matching trigger targets
findings.statement: `statement.contains(table)` rejected any trigger whose statement merely CONTAINED a pinned table name as a substring, e.g. `CREATE TRIGGER ... ON canonical_nodes_backup`, which targets neither pinned table. Legitimate recreate/backup trigger scaffolding failed the pin.
findings.assessment: GENUINE OVER-rejection. Reproduced at RED before fixing.
findings.fix: `targets_pinned_table` becomes `mentions_pinned_table`: it splits the statement on every character that cannot appear in an identifier (keeping `.` so a schema qualifier stays one token for `is_pinned_table` to strip) and compares TOKENS, the same way every other arm does. Same call site, same arm, no restructuring.
findings.anti_loosening_guarantee: Precision on the trigger TARGET did NOT cost the trigger BODY. Verified how the `;` split actually behaves rather than assuming: the FIRST body statement is NOT its own fragment — it stays glued to the `CREATE TRIGGER ...` head (the split point is the `;` that TERMINATES it), so the arm's whole-fragment token scan still sees `UPDATE canonical_nodes SET logical_id ...` there. Every LATER body statement IS its own fragment, judged independently by the UPDATE / INSERT arms. Both cases are pinned by pin_rejects_a_lookalike_trigger_whose_body_writes_a_canonical_logical_id (first-statement, later-statement, and schema-qualified variants).
findings.doc_correction: The doc comment's Known-limits paragraph previously claimed the trigger head and the body UPDATE are 'independently rejected' fragments. That was wrong for the FIRST body statement; the text now states the glue precisely.

finding.location_at_review: src/rust/crates/fathomdb-schema/src/lib.rs — every arm of statement_violates_logical_id_pin (each begins statement.starts_with(...))
finding.statement: SQLite's grammar allows an optional with-clause in FRONT of UPDATE / INSERT / DELETE, so `WITH x AS (SELECT 1) UPDATE canonical_nodes SET logical_id = 'y';` is a running forward-mint backfill whose normalised statement starts with WITH. It matched NO arm and was ACCEPTED by a TERMINAL-FOREVER pin.
finding.provenance: PRE-EXISTING: present at 2afd168c (the slice's first GREEN) and at every fix head; NOT introduced by fix-1 or fix-2. Same finding family as the two closed codex §9 [P2]s (leading-keyword-anchored extraction).
finding.assessment: GENUINE BYPASS. Reproduced at RED before fixing.
finding.fix: One new PRIVATE helper, writes_pinned_identity_anywhere(statement, names_column), called FIRST inside statement_violates_logical_id_pin and independent of the leading keyword. It refuses any statement that writes logical_id in an ASSIGNMENT position on a pinned table: (a) the ` SET ` clause (up to WHERE / FROM / RETURNING, via the existing set_clause helper) names logical_id AND some token of the statement is a pinned table (mentions_pinned_table, which already carries the fix-1 qualifier strip); or (b) the table after ` INTO ` IS pinned and the statement either names logical_id or omits the column list — the same rule the INSERT arm applies. NO CTE/paren parser was built.
finding.why_it_runs_first: Several keyword arms `return false` EARLY (e.g. an UPDATE whose target is not pinned), which would shadow a fallback placed at the end of the function. Running the catch-all first makes it a true catch-all; as a boolean OR the ordering is otherwise semantics-free.
finding.why_write_position_not_statement_shape: It closes the whole 'something displaces the leading keyword' family at once rather than only the WITH spelling, and it is the line the four shipped accepts already draw: they NAME logical_id in READ positions (predicate, index column list, column declaration) and never assign to it.

deliberate_over_rejections_introduced: A statement that assigns logical_id on a NON-pinned table while merely MENTIONING a pinned table anywhere (e.g. `WITH x AS (SELECT 1 FROM canonical_nodes) UPDATE other SET logical_id = …`, or `INSERT INTO other … FROM canonical_nodes ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET logical_id = …`) is now REFUSED. After an arbitrary prefix the update TARGET cannot be located token-wise without parsing. This is over-rejection by design (the pin's stated stance), it breaks nothing shipped, and it is cheap to work around honestly. The two paired controls bound it: a lookalike target and a canonical-table READ inside a CTE both stay ACCEPTED.
